Oh, Pluto, how they have defamed thee, for lo these four decades, or so. 
It just ain't right. 
Pluto has provided us all so much, whether educational material in the form of colorful classroom posters, or entertainment, or simply a sense of satisfaction and completion to generations upon generations of children and adults -- without asking a thing of us in return.
The unceremonious dumping of Pluto is one of the most inconsiderate and dare I say it callous  acts I have witnessed since ... well,  some of the stuff I  did in college that does not merit discussion in this space. 
The revised rules for planets that exclude Pluto ask questions like whether the body orbits the sun, or whatever, sciency-sounding hoo-ha; but fail to ask the most important question: has the astronomical body served us faithfully in its role as planet? 
To that question, Pluto can stand as proud as any Jupiter. Perhaps more, for to be the last of the list, the tiny timid sphere that served (/serves) as outpost to all of humanity's horizon is a noble and heroic effort that should be rewarded, not punished. 
We should not be delisting Pluto, we should be sending cookies, and an apology note, smeared with tears.

Somewhat surprised that none of our resident astro-geeks have commented on a certain aspect of the visual depiction that accompanies this puzzle.

The ORBITAL path of each of the planets is actually a (non-circular) ellipse. The Sun is not located at the geometric center of the orbit, but rather at one focus of the ellipse. That said, the true planetary ellipses are actually quite circular. The orbit of Venus is very close to perfectly circular (eccentricity ~ 0.0068), while that of Mercury is the least circular (eccentricity ~ 0.2056)---a perfect circle has eccentricity 0.

To my eye, the orbit depicted for Mercury (for example) is not centered around the (center of) the Sun---this is actually correct. But I can't say for sure if the depicted orbit is perfectly circular---which would be incorrect---or just a wee bit elliptical.

An earlier poster, whose post I can't find again, commented that they thought that Copernicus was holding an orrery not an astrolabe.  Here's what a Google picture search turns up.

This image shows a classic 1822 marble sculpture of the Renaissance astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus holding an armillary sphere and a pair of compasses.

I looked up armillary sphere and per Wikipedia:
An armillary sphere (variations are known as spherical astrolabe, armilla, or armil) is a model of objects in the sky (on the celestial sphere), consisting of a spherical framework of rings, centered on Earth or the Sun, that represent lines of celestial longitude and latitude and other astronomically important features, such as the ecliptic.
...
With the Earth as center, an armillary sphere is known as Ptolemaic. With the Sun as center, it is known as Copernican.

So, photo's caption is somewhat imprecise. 
And then there are orreries...
I find all of these things fascinating and some of the older ones are quite beautiful.

I have a huge grin on my face concerning all the consternation about Pluto's reclassification.  And it's not a smile of superiority (for once, 😉)--it's a smile of genuine affection for people who have strong feelings about Pluto.

I'm 74, and the books I read when I was a kid mentioned that there might be marshland vegetation on Mars.  And that Mercury always faced the sun.  And Jupiter had 12 moons and Saturn had 9.  (I should have known that they were talking about *known* moons.) It was that long ago.

I don't remember ever learning the planets' order...I don't remember not knowing them, so in love with astronomy was I at a very early age.  

And yet I just shrugged when Pluto was reclassified.  It never occurred to me that its feelings might be hurt.  Anthropomorphization never came to mind.

Nevertheless, I just love all the love that Pluto got, and is getting.
